source.title: Population codes for biological stereopsis extend beyond correlation-based binocular disparity computations
source.authors: B. G. Wundari; Ichiro Fujita; Hiroshi Ban

record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature overlap and unit selectivity in stereo-processing networks using feature dimensionality and monosemanticity, bearing on superposition geometry with methods applied to a different task and setting than the toy-model claim.
record.gate_note: The study applies superposition metrics to trained stereo networks and fMRI data. Behavioral depth judgments and disparity-prediction performance are not recorded as rows because they do not themselves measure the claim versions' representation geometry. Results cited from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study borrows superposition metrics (feature dimensionality from Toy Models; monosemantic score from Jermyn et al.) to compare stereo networks and fMRI voxels. The authors call this a diagnostic tool 'rather than as direct evidence for the underlying mechanism.' No result bears on whether any version holds. It does not vary sparsity or feature count against dimension, check near-orthogonal geometry, test importance-based allocation, examine alternative causes of polysemanticity, use SAEs or LLMs, or ask about feature dimensionality in the V6 sense. Its results compare architectures (correlation vs non-correlation binocular interactions) on metrics whose meaning presupposes the theory.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with additions. The authors conclude that correlation-based binocular computations represent features with stronger superposition, and that this interference may degrade population-level depth inference and human alignment. Only V3A, not V1, shows a population representation of reversed depth. Non-correlation (especially Concat) DNNs align best with humans. They propose that the brain combines correlation and non-correlation coding, and they treat superposition analysis as diagnostic rather than mechanistic evidence.
record.recipe_differences: Applies feature-dimensionality and monosemanticity measures associated with superposition research to stereo-processing networks and fMRI representations, rather than reproducing the original toy-model experiments. The study uses task-trained convolutional networks and controlled stimulus features.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured overlap differed by binocular interaction and network depth; SNN feature dimensionality declined across layers, and the interaction-by-layer effect was significant.

fits_no_version.finding: In shallow stereo CNNs, correlation-based binocular interactions (BEM, CMM) gave lower mean feature dimensionality than Concat and Sum-diff (differences 0.065–0.102, p<0.001). Feature dimensionality also declined from layer 1 upward.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The architectural form of input interaction (multiplicative vs additive/concatenative) changes how much superposition a task-trained network shows, as measured by Elhage-style feature dimensionality.

fits_no_version.finding: In GC-Net DNNs, the fraction of units monosemantic over controlled stimulus conditions rose with depth. The rise was steeper for Concat than for BEM, while CMM and Sum-diff did not differ from BEM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unit monosemanticity over task-relevant stimulus conditions increases with depth in task-trained vision networks, modulated by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Human fMRI voxel monosemanticity over disparity/density/correlation conditions increased from V1 toward V3A and higher areas (dorsal β=0.317, ventral β=0.457).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Voxel-level selectivity for disparity-related conditions increases along the human visual hierarchy.

record.code_released: https://github.com/hiroshiban/Retinotopy (retinotopy stimulus codes; study-model code not stated)
record.peer_reviewed: preprint (bioRxiv; the text says it was not certified by peer review)
record.problems: The feature-dimensionality and monosemanticity analyses use different measures; monosemanticity is explicitly indirect and restricted to controlled stimulus features. The fMRI measure is voxel-level and pools many neurons. The study does not test sparse co-activation or feature importance, and does not directly manipulate superposition to establish causality. Some plotted values are not numerically reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Behavioral RDS depth judgments, model disparity-prediction performance, and fMRI cross-decoding results were not included because they do not directly measure the representation geometries named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: All parts: sparse features exceeding dimensions, near-orthogonal overlap, sparsity-dependent transition, regular geometry. The feature dimensionality metric is applied but its premises are not tested.
Whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share; feature importance is never measured or varied.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
No LLMs and no dictionary/SAE recovery.
Features are assumed to be 1-D directions; multi-dimensional features are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Domain is visual neuroscience; superposition theory is imported as a measurement lens. The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1/V2 supports/limits_scope labels are not justified. The results compare binocular-interaction architectures; they do not test claims about superposition. The feature set for the monosemanticity score is 54 experimenter-defined stimulus conditions, not learned features. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures overlap-related geometry in stereo networks, but does not test sparse co-activation, a feature count exceeding dimensionality, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric configurations in toy models.
The study compares overlap-related measures across network architectures and depths, but does not test whether feature importance determines which features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test whether polysemantic units can arise without capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
No LLMs, feature-spread analyses in LLMs, or sparse features recovered by a dictionary are tested.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are tested.
The study defines features as directions in activation space but does not test whether the represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: SNN (BEM interaction)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on Monkaa for 10 epochs; 13 random seeds
rows.measure: Feature dimensionality; lower values indicate stronger superposition
rows.value: Lower feature dimensionality than Concat (mean-difference = 0.065, p < 0.001) and Sum-diff (mean-difference = 0.102, p < 0.001)
rows.note: The text reports the pairwise differences across all layers; strongest overlap was particularly in layer 3.
rows.check: Architecture comparison of feature dimensionality (BEM lower than Concat/Sum-diff). This uses the metric; it does not test V1's conditions (sparsity transition, more features than dims, geometry) or V2's importance allocation. The subject is a task-trained stereo CNN, not a toy model of superposition.

rows.subject: Human visual cortex
rows.operation_detail: Measured voxel monosemanticity across visual areas

conditions.value: V1, V2, V3, V3A, V3B, hV4, V7, hMT+

rows.measure: Monosemantic voxels per feature, used as an indirect index of superposition
rows.value: Monosemanticity increased from early to mid-higher visual areas; positive linear trends along dorsal (slope β = 0.317, p < 0.001) and ventral (β = 0.457, p < 0.001) pathways
rows.uncertainty: F(7, 147) = 21.804, p < 0.001; trend p-values as stated
rows.note: This is an indirect voxel-level measure; the authors caution that each voxel pools signals from hundreds of thousands of neurons.
rows.check: Voxel-level selectivity in human cortex is not superposition in a network. The authors say high voxel monosemanticity does not imply absence of cellular superposition.

rows.subject: DNN (BEM interaction)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on Monkaa for 10 epochs; 13 random seeds
rows.measure: Monosemanticity, an indirect index of superposition
rows.baseline: Reference slope for comparison with other interactions; absolute slope not stated
rows.value: Reference architecture; absolute monosemanticity slope not stated
rows.note: The authors report an overall increase with depth across DNNs, but do not give a separate absolute BEM slope.
rows.check: Not a result row: no value is reported. It serves only as the reference for the slope contrasts in R7–R9.

rows.subject: DNN (CMM interaction)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on Monkaa for 10 epochs; 13 random seeds
rows.operation_detail: Compared monosemanticity trend with BEM across network depth
rows.measure: Monosemanticity trend, an indirect index of superposition
rows.value: Slope difference from BEM: βCMM − βBEM = 0.0014, p = 0.148; not significantly different
rows.note: The nonsignificant difference does not establish that the absolute CMM trend is absent.
rows.check: Slope difference in monosemanticity versus BEM (0.0014, p=0.148). This is an architecture contrast on an indirect proxy computed over 54 controlled stimulus conditions, and it tests no version.
